narrative: The model estimates a 71% chance you will leave your job, so it treats you as a high retention risk; on that basis, the promotion is being denied. The strongest reason is your total years of experience: at 6–10 years, you are above the most common range among employees predicted to stay, most of whom have 1–5 years. That broader experience was the top signal pushing the prediction toward leaving. The second strongest signal was your time in your current organization, at 1–5 years. Although this tenure is common among stayers, in combination with your overall experience the model read it as increasing the likelihood of a move. The third most important factor worked in the opposite direction: you reported no other job opportunities. Lacking outside offers normally makes leaving less likely, so this reduced the risk, but it was not enough to offset the two experience signals. Because the model still sees a high chance of departure, the organization should consider whether a promotion would improve retention or whether a clearer development and recognition plan is needed. You may want to discuss career progression, support, and what would make you more likely to stay. The decision should be reviewed alongside your recent performance and retention options, not treated as a final judgment about your value.
